claim: Current data are consistent with rising levels of antibiotic resistance, and this trend is not restricted to particular pathogens or specific geographic settings.
source: Although the quality and completeness of surveillance is variable, current data are consistent with rising levels of resistance; this worrisome trend is not restricted to particular pathogens or specific geographic settings (WHO, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2014 surveillance data

claim: Antibiotic resistance causes up to 2 million serious infections, 23,000 deaths, and 35 billion dollars in losses in the United States alone.
source: While an accurate assessment of the current health and economic losses attributable to antibiotic resistance is elusive, the estimated numbers, ranging up to 2 million serious infections, 23,000 deaths, and 35 billion dollars in the United States alone, are staggering (CDC, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to CDC 2013 estimates

claim: Similar numbers of deaths have been attributed to antibiotic-resistant infections in Europe.
source: Similar numbers of deaths have been attributed to antibiotic-resistant infections in Europe (O'Neill, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Neill 2014

claim: Antimicrobial-resistant infections are projected to cause 10 million deaths and 100 trillion dollars in economic losses by 2050.
source: Most recently, a projection of 10 million deaths and 100 trillion dollars in economic losses attributable to antimicrobial-resistant infections by 2050 has been circulated (O'Neill, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Neill 2014 projection

claim: The conventional wisdom, often attributed to Paul Ehrlich, is that early and aggressive use of antimicrobial agents is most effective for optimizing cure and minimizing the risk of resistance.
source: The conventional wisdom guiding the rapidity and dosing of drugs, often attributed to Paul Ehrlich, (Ehrlich, 1913) is that early and aggressive use of antimicrobial agents is most effective for optimizing cure and minimizing the risk of resistance (Levin et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ehrlich 1913 and Levin et al. 1999

claim: Some researchers have suggested that more moderate approaches to antibiotic treatment may perform better than aggressive approaches for minimizing resistance.
source: Recently, there has been some debate as to the universality of the claim that these aggressive approaches are optimal for minimizing the risk of resistance, with some researchers suggesting that more moderate approaches may perform better (Read et al., 2011) and others defending the standard approach (Ankomah and Levin, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Read et al. 2011 and Ankomah and Levin 2014

claim: Early high dose treatment will most rapidly reduce the size of the microbial population from which drug-resistant isolates appear and thus minimize the probability of the emergence of resistance during treatment.
source: A central rationale for an aggressive approach is that early high dose treatment will most rapidly reduce the size of the microbial population from which drug-resistant isolates appear and thus minimize the probability of the emergence of resistance during treatment (Bonhoeffer et al., 1997; Knudsen et al., 2003; Wiuff et al., 2003; Tam et al., 2005, 2007; D'Agata et al., 2007; Ankomah and Levin, 2014; Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to theoretical and modeling studies

claim: Higher doses of antibiotics impose stronger selective pressure which drives a more rapid emergence of resistance.
source: In contrast, the rationale for a more moderate approach is that higher doses of antibiotics impose stronger selective pressure which drives a more rapid emergence of resistance (Read and Huijben, 2009; Read et al., 2011; Kouyos et al., 2014), and that rapid suppression of drug-susceptible isolates may allow for competitive release of existing drug-resistant isolates (de Roode et al., 2004; Wargo et al., 2007; Huijben et al., 2010; Pena-Miller et al., 2013; Pollitt et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on selection pressure and competitive release

claim: Rapid suppression of drug-susceptible isolates may allow for competitive release of existing drug-resistant isolates.
source: In contrast, the rationale for a more moderate approach is that higher doses of antibiotics impose stronger selective pressure which drives a more rapid emergence of resistance (Read and Huijben, 2009; Read et al., 2011; Kouyos et al., 2014), and that rapid suppression of drug-susceptible isolates may allow for competitive release of existing drug-resistant isolates (de Roode et al., 2004; Wargo et al., 2007; Huijben et al., 2010; Pena-Miller et al., 2013; Pollitt et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on competitive release

claim: Optimal dosing strategies for the prevention of resistance in individuals are not necessarily optimal for limiting resistance at the population level.
source: From a theoretical perspective, optimal dosing strategies for the prevention of resistance in individuals are not necessarily optimal for limiting resistance at the population level (Lipsitch and Samore, 2002; Mills et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lipsitch and Samore 2002 and Mills et al. 2013

claim: The extent of effective competition between drug-susceptible and drug-resistant isolates is a key determinant of whether an aggressive approach is better than a moderate approach for hosts being treated for disease.
source: We demonstrate that the extent of effective competition between drug-susceptible and drug-resistant isolates is a key determinant of whether an aggressive approach is better (in terms of resistance prevention) than a moderate approach for hosts being treated for disease.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the modeling results presented

claim: Even within a model that allows for very strong competition, different realistic combinations of parameter values can support the aggressive or moderate approach as optimal.
source: Most importantly, we find that even within a model that allows for very strong competition, different realistic combinations of parameter values can support the aggressive or moderate approach as optimal.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis presented in the study

claim: The within-host model includes both wild-type (drug-sensitive; DS) bacteria and drug-resistant (DR) bacteria which arise by some presumably rare mechanism from the drug-sensitive type.
source: The model includes both wild-type (drug-sensitive; DS) bacteria and drug-resistant (DR) bacteria which arise by some presumably rare mechanism from the drug-sensitive type.
evidence: This describes the structure of the within-host model

claim: The mechanism of resistance acquisition could be single-point mutation, acquisition of resistance genes through horizontal gene transfer, or another mechanism.
source: This mechanism could be single-point mutation, acquisition of resistance genes through horizontal gene transfer, or another mechanism (Lipsitch and Samore, 2002; zur Wiesch et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lipsitch and Samore 2002 and zur Wiesch et al. 2011

claim: The mechanisms of resistance and their probabilities affect the relative importance of de novo resistance compared to pre-existing resistance circulating in a population.
source: While we do not explictly model these differences, we note that the mechanisms of resistance and their probabilities affect the relative importance of de novo resistance compared to pre-existing resistance circulating in a population (Lipsitch and Samore, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lipsitch and Samore 2002

claim: In the within-host model, each strain initiates an immune response which follows density-dependent kinetics.
source: In our model, each strain initiates an immune response which follows density-dependent kinetics.
evidence: This describes a feature of the within-host model structure

claim: Bacteria grow in a resource-dependent manner and have a death rate which increases under higher antibiotic concentrations.
source: Bacteria grow in a resource-dependent manner and have a death rate which increases under higher antibiotic concentrations.
evidence: This describes features of the within-host model structure

claim: The DR strain is assumed to have a slower growth rate reflecting fitness costs associated with mutation or acquisition of resistance genes.
source: The DR strain, by definition, has a higher minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) than the DS strain and is assumed to have a slower growth rate reflecting fitness costs associated with mutation or acquisition of resistance genes.
evidence: This is an assumption built into the model structure based on biological knowledge

claim: Strains compete for resources in the within-host model.
source: The strain interactions in the model are complex: strains compete for resources, and each strain can suppress the other by triggering a host immune response.
evidence: This describes the competitive interactions in the within-host model

claim: Each strain can suppress the other by triggering a host immune response in the within-host model.
source: The strain interactions in the model are complex: strains compete for resources, and each strain can suppress the other by triggering a host immune response.
evidence: This describes the competitive interactions in the within-host model

claim: The DS strain benefits the DR strain as DR is generated from the DS population through acquired resistance.
source: However, the DS strain also benefits the DR strain as DR is generated from the DS population through acquired resistance.
evidence: This describes an interaction in the within-host model

claim: 60,000 sets of parameters were drawn from ranges containing the values used previously by Ankomah and Levin (2014).
source: To explore these complex interactions, we drew 60,000 sets of parameters from ranges containing the values used previously (Ankomah and Levin, 2014) (see Table 1), spanning a range of strengths of the immune system (ki, kp, η, α), relative overall fitness of the DR strain (Λr, Mr), pre-existing DR bacilli, the growth rate of the DS strain (Λs), and the mutation parameter μ.
evidence: This describes the computational methodology used in the study

claim: Parameter sets in which resistance levels were negatively correlated (S < −0.7) with antibiotic dosage were classed as 'aggressive is best'.
source: Accordingly, parameter sets in which resistance levels were negatively (S < −0.7) or positively (S > 0.7) correlated with antibiotic dosage as determined by the Spearman correlation S were classed as 'aggressive is best' or 'moderate is best'; other results were classed as neutral.
evidence: This describes the classification methodology used in the study

claim: Parameter sets in which resistance levels were positively correlated (S > 0.7) with antibiotic dosage were classed as 'moderate is best'.
source: Accordingly, parameter sets in which resistance levels were negatively (S < −0.7) or positively (S > 0.7) correlated with antibiotic dosage as determined by the Spearman correlation S were classed as 'aggressive is best' or 'moderate is best'; other results were classed as neutral.
evidence: This describes the classification methodology used in the study

claim: The between-host model was developed with four host compartments: susceptible, infected with DS (X), infected with DR (Y) and dually infected (D).
source: To explore a wide range of inter-strain interactions at the population level, we developed a model with four host compartments: susceptible, infected with DS (X), infected with DR (Y) and dually infected (D).
evidence: This describes the structure of the between-host model

claim: Distinct pathogens may be entirely independent of each other, not interacting directly or indirectly.
source: At one of the continuum, we posit that distinct pathogens may be entirely independent of each other, not interacting directly or indirectly (e.g., through immune modulation or resource competition).
evidence: This describes one end of the continuum of inter-strain interactions in the between-host model

claim: Very similar strains of the same pathogen are likely to be competing for hosts.
source: At the other end of the continuum, very similar strains of the same pathogen are likely to be competing for hosts.
evidence: This describes the other end of the continuum of inter-strain interactions in the between-host model

claim: In the competing model, decreasing the DS strain paves the way for an increase in resistance by removing the DR strain's competitor, despite the fact that decreasing DS also removes a source of resistance.
source: In the competing model (top row), decreasing the DS strain (X) paves the way for an increase in resistance (Y) by removing the DR strain's competitor, despite the fact that decreasing DS also removes a source of resistance.
evidence: This is explained in the text and illustrated in Figure 1

claim: If the strains are not competing, reducing DS reduces DR by reducing a source of resistance.
source: In contrast, if the strains are not competing (bottom row), including not competing for hosts, hosts must be able to harbor both infections (duals, D). In this case, reducing DS reduces DR by reducing a source of resistance.
evidence: This is explained in the text and illustrated in Figure 1

claim: The between-host model incorporates competition and independence, parameterized by a 'similarity coefficient' that smoothly moves from one to the other.
source: Our between-host model incorporates competition and independence, parameterized by a 'similarity coefficient' that smoothly moves from one to the other (see Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the between-host model structure

claim: When c = 1 the strains are highly similar and neutral in the sense of Lipsitch et al. (2009) if they are identical.
source: When c = 1 the strains are highly similar and neutral in the sense of Lipsitch et al. (2009) if they are identical.
evidence: This describes the behavior of the similarity coefficient in the between-host model

claim: When c = 0, the two strains act independently; infection with one does not affect the spread of the other.
source: When c = 0, the two strains act independently; infection with one does not affect the spread of the other.
evidence: This describes the behavior of the similarity coefficient in the between-host model

claim: The best policy for reducing the amount of resistance in both models can be either aggressive or moderate despite the fact that both models capture potentially strong competition and the acquisition of de novo resistance.
source: The best policy for reducing the amount of resistance in both models can be either aggressive or moderate despite the fact that both models capture potentially strong competition and the acquisition of de novo resistance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the modeling results

claim: The choice of best approach depends on the combined effect of the complex set of inter-strain interactions.
source: The choice of best approach depends on the combined effect of the complex set of inter-strain interactions, and typically, one of these approaches is the clear winner (see Appendix figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis

claim: Whether treatment increases or decreases resistance over the course of infection depends on many of the parameters in the model.
source: Whether treatment increases or decreases resistance over the course of infection depends on many of the parameters in the model.
evidence: This is a finding from the sensitivity analysis

claim: The relationship between resistance and dosage is relatively robust to variation in each parameter alone, but small changes in several parameters can have a radical effect.
source: We found that the relationship is relatively robust to variation in each parameter alone, but that small changes in several parameters can have a radical effect.
evidence: This is a finding from the sensitivity analysis

claim: No single parameter determines whether aggressive or moderate treatment minimizes resistance.
source: No single parameter determines whether aggressive or moderate treatment minimizes resistance.
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter analysis

claim: A relatively small change in several parameters can shift the model from one mode to the other.
source: A relatively small change in several parameters can shift the model from one mode to the other.
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter analysis

claim: The number of pre-existing resistant cells affects the outcome of whether aggressive or moderate treatment minimizes resistance.
source: The number of pre-existing resistant cells affects the outcome (coefficient 0.79).
evidence: This is a finding from the DAPC analysis

claim: When pre-existing numbers of resistant cells are low (<10), parameters which lead to a 'moderate' policy being best include higher growth rate of the DR and DS strains, lower immune parameters, and a higher MIC of the DR strain.
source: When pre-existing numbers are low (<10), parameters which lead to a 'moderate' policy to be best include higher growth rate of the DR and DS strains (ΛR, 1.4 and ΛS, 0.92), lower immune parameters kp and η (−0.74; −0.66) and a higher MIC of the DR strain (mR; 0.34).
evidence: This is a finding from the DAPC analysis

claim: An aggressive approach is preferred when the immune system is relatively strong (higher values of immune parameters kp, η).
source: In other words, we find that an aggressive approach is preferred when the immune system is relatively strong (higher values of immune parameters kp, η), and when the DR strain has a relatively low growth rate (ΛR) and low MIC (mr).
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter analysis

claim: An aggressive approach is preferred when the DR strain has a relatively low growth rate and low MIC.
source: In other words, we find that an aggressive approach is preferred when the immune system is relatively strong (higher values of immune parameters kp, η), and when the DR strain has a relatively low growth rate (ΛR) and low MIC (mr).
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter analysis

claim: If there is pre-existing resistance, the immune system is weaker, and/or the growth rate or MIC higher, a moderate approach minimizes resistance.
source: Conversely, if there is pre-existing resistance, the immune system is weaker, and/or the growth rate or MIC higher, a moderate approach minimizes resistance.
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter analysis

claim: Pre-existing populations of DR pathogens favor a moderate approach, since there is no possibility that a hard-and-fast approach will clear the infection before resistance can arise.
source: Pre-existing populations of DR pathogens (i.e., resistance that appears prior to exposure to treatment) favor a moderate approach, since there is no possibility that a hard-and-fast approach will clear the infection before resistance can arise.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results

claim: A higher DR growth rate generally leads to a moderate policy being best, but this can be offset with a strong immune system keeping both strains in check.
source: These figures reveal a few intuitive trade-offs: a higher DR growth rate (ΛR) generally leads to a moderate policy being best (light blue; positive correlation between treatment and DR), but this can be offset with a strong immune system keeping both strains in check (high η or high kp).
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter analysis illustrated in Figure 4

claim: A higher DR growth rate or a higher MIC make the DR strain a robust competitor and consequently favor a moderate policy.
source: A higher DR growth rate or a higher MIC (mR) make the DR strain a robust competitor and also consequently favors a moderate policy.
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter analysis illustrated in Figure 4

claim: While the mutation rate affects the overall numbers of DR bacteria, it does not have a strong effect on the relationship between treatment and total resistance.
source: Interestingly, while the mutation rate affects the overall numbers of DR bacteria (particularly in cases when they are not present initially), it does not have a strong effect on the relationship between treatment and total resistance.
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter analysis

claim: If resistant cells are present initially, then they do not need to emerge by (rare) mutation or acquisition mechanisms from the sensitive strain.
source: If resistant cells are present initially, then they do not need to emerge by (rare) mutation or acquisition mechanisms from the sensitive strain.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the model dynamics

claim: A 'moderate is best', or neutral conclusion is much more likely with pre-existing resistance, keeping everything else the same.
source: This simple observation has consequences for our analysis; a 'moderate is best', or neutral conclusion is much more likely with pre-existing resistance, keeping everything else the same.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis

claim: When there is no pre-existing resistance, the DR strain must have a higher MIC, higher growth rate and face a weaker immune system in order to be a robust competitor than it does when it is present initially.
source: When there is no pre-existing resistance, the DR strain must have a higher MIC, higher growth rate and face a weaker immune system in order to be a robust competitor than it does when it is present initially.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis

claim: There is strong opportunity for competition between strains encoded in the within-host model through shared resources and through the triggering of an immune response that suppresses both strains equally.
source: There is strong opportunity for competition between strains encoded in the model; competition plays out through shared resources which may be limiting as well as through the triggering of an immune response that suppresses both strains equally.
evidence: This describes features of the within-host model structure

claim: Both resource competition and immune-mediated competition occur when bacterial populations are large.
source: Both of these effects occur when bacterial populations are large.
evidence: This is an inference about the model dynamics

claim: The initial appearance of resistance depends critically on the presence of drug-sensitive organisms.
source: However, the initial appearance of resistance also depends critically on the presence of drug-sensitive organisms.
evidence: This is an inference about the model dynamics

claim: Effective competition naturally requires a DR strain that has the capacity to be a robust competitor to the DS progenitor.
source: In particular, effective competition naturally requires a DR strain that has the capacity to be a robust competitor to the DS progenitor.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results

claim: A DR strain can be a robust competitor by maintaining a strong growth capacity in the presence of antibiotic treatment or immune pressure, or by facing an immune system that is not particularly strong.
source: This can be achieved in two ways: it can maintain a strong growth capacity in the presence of antibiotic treatment or immune pressure, or it can face an immune system that is not particularly strong.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results

claim: These findings are not an artifact of the model structure, and they will likely occur in any model that includes de novo appearance of resistant strains and where resistant strains can compete for resources with their drug-sensitive cousins.
source: These findings are not an artifact of the model structure, and indeed they will likely occur in any model that includes de novo appearance of resistant strains by mutation or acquisition of resistance determinants by drug-sensitive organisms, and where resistant strains can then compete for resources with their drug-sensitive cousins.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generalizability of the findings

claim: Effective competition can be described as the net extent to which a decrease in one strain benefits the other.
source: Effective competition can be described as the net extent to which a decrease in one strain benefits the other.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors

claim: The formulation of effective competition used in the study is a good predictor of whether treatment increases resistance, with an area under the receiver–operator characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.94.
source: Nevertheless, this formulation of effective competition is a good predictor of whether treatment, when added, increases resistance. We used it to classify whether treatment would increase or decrease resistance, and found that the classification worked well, with an area under the receiver–operator characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.94 (the theoretical maximum is 1, and a classifier that guesses randomly has AUC of 0.5).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of effective competition

claim: The between-host model has the possibility of three distinct steady states: no disease, both DS and DR present, and only the DR strain present.
source: The model has the possibility of three distinct steady states (equilibria): no disease, both DS and DR present, and only the DR strain present.
evidence: This describes the mathematical properties of the between-host model

claim: If there were no acquisition of resistance, there would also be the possibility of an equilibrium with only the DS strain.
source: If there were no acquisition of resistance, there would also be the possibility of an equilibrium with only the DS strain.
evidence: This describes the mathematical properties of the between-host model

claim: The stability region of the DR-only equilibrium changes as the similarity coefficient increases.
source: Figure 5 shows that the stability region of the DR-only equilibrium changes as the similarity coefficient increases.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5

claim: When c = 0, the DR-only equilibrium is invaded by the DS strain as soon as R01 > 1.
source: When c = 0, the DR-only equilibrium is invaded by the DS strain as soon as R01 > 1 (vertical blue line).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5

claim: When the strains are more similar, R01 must be higher in order to invade the DR-only equilibrium.
source: However, when the strains are more similar, R01 must be higher in order to invade, and when c = 1, there is no equilibrium DS prevalence unless R01 ≥ R02.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5

claim: Treatment decreases resistance when the R0 values of both strains are relatively low, the rate of acquisition of resistance is high and the similarity coefficient is low.
source: Appendix figure 9, Figures 6, 7 illustrate how the best policy depends on the fitness of the DR strain and the other parameters. Treatment decreases resistance when the R0 values of both strains are relatively low, the rate of acquisition of resistance is high and the similarity coefficient is low.
evidence: This is a finding from the between-host model analysis

claim: The strongest driver of a moderate policy being best is a high similarity coefficient (c, coefficient 0.93).
source: Here, the strongest driver of a moderate policy being best is a high similarity coefficient (c, coefficient 0.93).
evidence: This is a finding from the DAPC analysis of the between-host model

claim: High R02 and R01 contribute to a moderate policy being best.
source: High R02 and R01 (coefficients 1.01, 0.65) contribute, as does a low acquisition rate (coefficient −0.56).
evidence: This is a finding from the DAPC analysis of the between-host model

claim: The rate of competitive release does not contribute to the DAPC weighting in the between-host model.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, the rate of competitive release does not contribute to the DAPC weighting (−0.02).
evidence: This is a finding from the DAPC analysis of the between-host model

claim: An aggressive strategy is more likely to minimize resistance when the DR strain is relatively unfit (low R02), and the DR population is supported by a high rate of acquisition.
source: An aggressive strategy is more likely to minimize resistance when the DR strain is relatively unfit (low R02), and the DR population is supported by a high rate of acquisition.
evidence: This is a finding from the between-host model analysis

claim: An aggressive strategy is likely to be best when the strains are more independent (a low similarity coefficient).
source: Furthermore, an aggressive strategy is likely to be best when the strains are more independent (a low similarity coefficient).
evidence: This is a finding from the between-host model analysis

claim: Independence means that even a relatively unfit strain can be transmitted in the population, despite the presence of a more fit strain, because when strains are independent they can each super-infect hosts already infected with the other strain.
source: Independence means that even a relatively unfit strain can be transmitted in the population, despite the presence of a more fit strain, because when strains are independent they can each super-infect hosts already infected with the other strain, and they can be transmitted from those with dual infection (if these cannot happen then the strains cannot be independent; rather, they would compete for hosts and/or for infectivity).
evidence: This is an explanation of the model dynamics

claim: Co-infection can, but does not always, allow DR strains to persist in the long term where they would not be able to do so otherwise.
source: We noted previously (Colijn et al., 2009) that such co-infection can, but does not always, allow DR strains to persist in the long term where they would not be able to do so otherwise; similar results were recently reported by Hansen and Day (2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Colijn et al. 2009 and Hansen and Day 2014

claim: The effects of co-infection on DR persistence are a result of the level of competition and are not a consequence of co-infection itself.
source: Our current results clarify that these effects are a result of the level of competition and are not a consequence of co-infection.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study

claim: Co-infection can be present under high, low, or intermediate levels of competition.
source: Co-infection can be present under high, low, or intermediate levels of competition.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results

claim: The factors that favor an aggressive policy—lower R02, higher rates of resistance acquisition and increased independence between strains—have the net impact of reducing inter-strain competition.
source: The factors that favor an aggressive policy—lower R02, higher rates of resistance acquisition and increased independence between strains—have the net impact of reducing inter-strain competition.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from the between-host model

claim: A low R01 makes an aggressive approach more likely to be preferred because competition for hosts is low when there are plenty of susceptible hosts.
source: A low R01 also makes an aggressive approach more likely to be preferred (see Appendix figure 9); competition for hosts is low when there are plenty of susceptible hosts, whether the model has strict competition mechanisms or not. This occurs when both R0 values are low.
evidence: This is a finding from the between-host model analysis

claim: Low R02 means the DR strain is not a fit competitor.
source: Low R02 means the DR strain is not a fit competitor, a high independence (1 − c) explicitly reduces competition through protection from re-infection and through independent recovery, and a higher mutation rate increases the benefit the DR strain enjoys from DS.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model dynamics

claim: The measure of effective competition in the between-host model is a good predictor of the effect of treatment (AUC 0.94).
source: As in the within-host model, this measure of effective competition is a good predictor of the effect of treatment (AUC 0.94; Appendix figure 10).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of effective competition in the between-host model

claim: Even where competitive release does not occur at all (r = 0), successful treatment of individuals drives population-level resistance when strains are competing.
source: Even where this does not occur at all (r = 0), successful treatment of individuals drives population-level resistance when strains are competing.
evidence: This is a finding from the between-host model analysis

claim: Treatment (reducing R01) moves the system to the left on the invasion plot, increasing resistance if there is effective competition at the between-host level.
source: Treatment (reducing R01) moves the system to the left on the invasion plot (Figure 5C), increasing resistance if there is effective competition at the between-host level.
evidence: This is explained in the text and illustrated in Figure 5C

claim: An aggressive policy for antibiotic treatment is preferred when the appearance and persistence of DR is driven by the existence of a sufficiently large DS population.
source: An aggressive policy for antibiotic treatment is preferred when the appearance and persistence of DR is driven by the existence of a sufficiently large DS population.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study

claim: In settings where aggressive policy is preferred, the benefits to the DR population which accrue from the acquisition of resistance from DS outweigh the costs of competition from a larger DS population.
source: In these settings, the benefits to the DR population which accrue from the acquisition of resistance from DS outweigh the costs of competition from a larger DS population.
evidence: This is an explanation of why aggressive policy is preferred in certain settings

claim: A moderate dosing policy is preferred when the DR strain is a fit enough competitor that acquisition of resistance plays a sufficiently small role in the DR population dynamics.
source: In contrast, a moderate dosing policy is preferred when the DR strain is a fit enough competitor that acquisition of resistance plays a sufficiently small role in the DR population dynamics.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study

claim: When moderate policy is preferred, the cost of competition from the DS population outweighs the benefit of additional DR bacteria appearing through acquired resistance.
source: Here, the cost of competition from the DS population outweighs the benefit of additional DR bacteria appearing through acquired resistance.
evidence: This is an explanation of why moderate policy is preferred in certain settings

claim: Both modes (aggressive and moderate being optimal) occur in models containing acquisition of resistance and competition.
source: Both modes occur in models containing acquisition of resistance and competition, and a small change in parameters can shift models from one mode to the other.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study

claim: Understanding why previous models and theory have differed in support of aggressive and moderate approaches requires evaluating both structural assumptions and parameter choices.
source: Understanding why previous models and theory have differed in support of aggressive (Ehrlich, 1913; Knudsen et al., 2003; Wiuff et al., 2003; Tam et al., 2005; D'Agata et al., 2007; Ankomah and Levin, 2014; Kim et al., 2014) and moderate (de Roode et al., 2004; Wargo et al., 2007; Gullberg et al., 2011; Huijben et al., 2013) approaches requires evaluating both structural assumptions and parameter choices (Spicknall et al., 2013) as these together affect the strength of effective competition between DR and DS strains.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, supported by citations to previous work

claim: In Ankomah and Levin (2014), at their chosen parameter values, there is little effective competition between DR and DS strains and they found an aggressive policy to be best.
source: In Ankomah and Levin (2014), the model structure incorporates complex interactions between strains, allowing for many facets of competition to be explored. At their chosen parameter values, however, there is little effective competition between DR and DS strains and they found an aggressive policy to be best.
evidence: This is an analysis of previous work by Ankomah and Levin 2014

claim: In Kim et al. (2014), DR strains had two alleles with no onward fitness evolution, little in-host competition, and low DR fitness; consequently, they found that an aggressive approach would be best.
source: In a recent work by Kim et al. (2014), DR strains had two alleles with no onward fitness evolution, little in-host competition, and low DR fitness; consequently, they also found that an aggressive approach would be best.
evidence: This is an analysis of previous work by Kim et al. 2014

claim: Gomes et al. (2013) assumed that there was competition for resources at high bacterial populations, and concluded that this competition could play a role in suppression of resistant strains.
source: Another recent model (Gomes et al., 2013) assumed that there was competition for resources at high bacterial populations, and concluded that this competition could play a role in suppression of resistant strains.
evidence: This is a summary of previous work by Gomes et al. 2013

claim: Geli et al. (2012) found that strong immunity supports an aggressive policy, but that selection was most intensive at intermediate strengths of treatment in chronic infections.
source: Work by Geli et al. (2012) explored different ecological dynamics and found that strong immunity supports an aggressive policy, but that selection was most intensive at intermediate strengths of treatment in chronic infections (Geli et al., 2012; Kouyos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of previous work by Geli et al. 2012

claim: Gullberg et al. (2011) found that even low concentrations of antibiotic can rapidly enrich DR sub-populations.
source: Gullberg et al. (2011) found that even low concentrations of antibiotic (where the DR and DS fitness may not differ) can rapidly enrich DR sub-populations.
evidence: This is a summary of previous work by Gullberg et al. 2011

claim: Huijben et al. (2013) found experimentally that competitive release of (pre-existing and relatively fit) resistant strains increased with increasing drug pressure.

claim: Both aggressive and moderate perspectives on antibiotic treatment are reasonable.

claim: Even in a system where aggressive approaches are most frequently best (the within-host model), a moderate approach can be preferred if the DR strain is slightly more fit and the environment is slightly more permissive.
source: We find that even in a system where aggressive approaches are most frequently best (the within-host model, based on Ankomah and Levin (2014)), a moderate approach can be preferred if the DR strain is slightly more fit and the environment is slightly more permissive; in this case, inter-strain competition mechanisms, which are always present, are more effective.
evidence: This is a finding from the within-host model analysis

claim: At the between-host level where herd-level competition effects might be expected to play out, even where competition mechanisms are strong, an aggressive approach may be best if one or both strains have a low basic reproduction number or if the rate of acquisition of resistance is high.

claim: Low basic reproduction numbers and high acquisition rates limit the effective competition between strains.

claim: In most circumstances, DR and DS variants of a single pathogen compete quite strongly because they will be closely related and likely share antigenic properties and induce a similar host immune response.

claim: Models have typically reflected competition for host resources or via a carrying capacity, such that competition takes place at high bacterial populations.

claim: Identical strains are expected to compete.

claim: The extent of competition is a key driver of how the balance between multiple strains changes in response to interventions.
